docs.title: How to read this master sheet
docs.text:
• This is a cross-sector navigation table, not an absolute ranking list that compares banks, platforms, semiconductors, and pharma on one single multiple.
  • A true Buy / Hold / Sell needs to be established in each sector page first, then prioritized here across themes.
  • Intraday moves provide only weak sentiment input and are insufficient alone to change action.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• Small dots = single companies; bubble labels = sector centers.
  • X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • Higher right and upper means stronger pros and more controllable costs; lower left means a weaker current setup.
  • Note: In the all-market chart, valuation_setup is still a relative score inside each sector basket, not a cross-sector unified multiple comparison.
  • For company-level comparison, use the per-theme charts and tables below as reference.

docs.title: Financial Institutions and Capital Markets - Comparison and Scores
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 17:36 CEST Parent page: Financial Institutions and Capital Markets Method page: Methods and Sources Scoring input: 2026-04-16 Market Snapshot（源文件保留在私有研究库）

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• Banks, alternative asset management, and payment networks cannot be measured with the same ruler; we first review earnings quality and regulatory sensitivity, then multiples.
  • Payment networks can tolerate higher valuation when quality is high; bank “cheapness” must be interpreted together with credit and capital requirements.
  • Names with high geography and restructuring variance will not move to Buy quickly even if multiples are low.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the more controlled the costs in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. APO — Buy — The permanent capital + private credit engine is most complete; valuation has not become distorted yet.
  2. V — Buy — Best quality and the hardest business model in this group, and although not cheap, still a long-duration top-tier in the financial basket.
  3. JPM — Hold — Most stable large-bank sample, but regulatory discount makes it more of a quality anchor than the strongest elastic buy.
  4. BAC — Hold — Valuation is cheap, but quality and earnings elasticity are still slightly behind JPM.
  5. BX — Hold — Platform breadth is strong, but volatility transmits more directly when exit and fundraising cycles turn against it.
  6. GS — Hold — Cyclical elasticity is clear, but success still depends on stronger capital-market activity.
  7. HSBC — Sell — Geography and restructuring variables are too many, so even at modest valuation risk/reward is not the best.

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• This group is better judged on P/S, earnings path, stability of funding sources, and credit-risk exposure rather than just current momentum.
  • Intraday moves are only a weak input; higher volatility does not mean a better setup.
  • Higher platformization and lower reliance on external financing appetite drives higher risk-control scores.

docs.title: Current ranking

docs.title: Pharma and Biotechnology - Comparison and Scores
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 17:36 CEST Parent page: Pharma and Biotechnology Method page: Methods and Sources Scoring input: 2026-04-16 Market Snapshot（源文件保留在私有研究库）

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• First separate mature pharma, platform biotech, and healthcare service integrators before comparing valuation and growth.
  • High growth is not automatically Buy; pipeline, patent cliffs, policy margin pressure, and supply capability must all be considered together.
  • CVS — CVS Health has a different business model and is treated as a healthcare service/insurance integrator separately.

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• Compare platform control, distribution power, and AI monetization pathways first, then valuation multiples; one megacap being more expensive does not automatically push it to the bottom.
  • Valuation is based mainly on a mix of forward PE + P/S, avoiding single-multiple comparisons between AMZN’s capital-heavy platform and AAPL’s mature hardware platform.
  • TSLA — Tesla remains in this basket, but as a conditional name it is first given a risk discount.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the more controlled the costs in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. MSFT — Buy — Enterprise distribution control and the Azure AI monetization path are the clearest; despite a premium, it remains the highest-conviction core slot in the platform basket.
  2. AMZN — Buy — The AWS + ads + retail triple-engine is still working, and on a platform-basket basis this valuation is not the most constraining.
  3. GOOG — Buy — Search cash flow provides enough cushion, and Cloud AI continues to improve the growth structure, making value-for-cash balance comparatively reasonable.
  4. META — Buy — The ad engine and AI efficiency gains are both paying off, but high CapEx and regulatory pressure keep it slightly below the most stable platform spot.
  5. AAPL — Hold — Quality is exceptional, but it currently acts more like a mature platform defensive holding; the further acceleration of AI-driven device replacement still needs confirmation.
  6. TSLA — Sell — Long-dated optionality is large, but the mismatch between auto cash flow and very high valuation is still the hardest-to-manage risk in this group.

docs.title: Semiconductors and Foundational Compute - Comparison and Scores
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-06-06 CEST Parent page: Semiconductors and Foundational Compute Method page: Methods and Sources Scoring input: 2026-04-16 Market Snapshot（源文件保留在私有研究库）

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• First separate platform compute, manufacturing backbone, memory cycle, and edge/analog, then do relative valuation.
  • A cheap cyclical stock does not automatically win over a scarce platform; scarcity, realization certainty, and geo/geopolitical execution risk must be considered together.
  • Conditional and transition names are given risk discounts by default, and only pulled back when valuation is exceptionally strong.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the better cost control in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. NVDA — Buy — Platform position is strongest; even if it is not cheap, it remains the hardest-to-replace core thesis in this group.
  2. TSM — Buy — Advanced manufacturing and packaging infrastructure are scarce, and current valuation can still be partly offset by a geography discount.
  3. AVGO — Hold / staged pullback-buy only — Custom XPU plus networking duration remains first-tier, but after Q2 FY2026 the provisional line stack is 420 / 450 / 480 / 525; no fresh chase.
  4. MU — Hold — HBM tailwind is clearest, but the strong cyclical nature of memory means this is a high-quality cyclical basket rather than a long-horizon best-in-class core.
  5. QCOM — Hold / no-chase — Physical AI and data-center inference optionality are stronger than the old edge-AI frame, but the current price is already in the no-chase zone and it is still not a core AI-infrastructure leader.
  6. AMD — Hold — The second-position thesis is valid, but software ecosystem scale and monetization ramp still need to be proven.
  7. TXN — Hold — Quality is solid, but AI resilience is limited; more of a base position than a front-line pick in this group.
  8. MRVL — Hold — High upside and high concentration, odds are decent but value still trails the leaders and infrastructure layer.
  9. ARM — Sell — Scarcity is strong, but current valuation already discounts too many positive outcomes early, so margin of safety is thin.
  10. INTC — Sell — Transformation upside is large, but triple execution risk across product, manufacturing, and capex remains highest in this group.
  11. SNDK — Sell — More like a NAND cycle trade than an AI core thesis; the standalone sample window is still too short.

docs.title: Buy
docs.text:
• NVDA: Platform position is strongest; even if not cheap, still the hardest-to-replace core thesis in this group.
  • TSM: Advanced manufacturing and advanced packaging base is scarce, and current valuation can still be partly offset by a geography discount.
  • AVGO: Custom XPU + networking duration remains strong, but Q2 FY2026 provisional lines are now 420 / 450 / 480 / 525; keep Hold core / staged pullback-buy only.

docs.title: Hold
docs.text:
• MU: HBM tailwind is the clearest, but memory’s strong cyclical profile means this is a high-quality cycle stock rather than the long-duration best solution.
  • QCOM: Terminal AI odds are decent and valuation is not expensive, but it remains conditional edge compute rather than a core line.
  • AMD: The second-position story is valid, but software ecosystem scale and realization at volume still need confirmation.
  • TXN: Quality is strong but AI elasticity is limited, making it more a base hold than this group’s front runner.
  • MRVL: High elasticity and high concentration together; odds are decent but value lags leaders and platform foundations.

docs.title: Sell
docs.text:
• ARM: Scarcity is strong, but valuation has already baked in too many good-news headlines, leaving little margin of safety.
  • INTC: Transformation upside is large, but execution risk across product, manufacturing, and capex is still too high.
  • SNDK: More like a NAND cycle ticket than an AI core theme, and the standalone sample is still too short.

docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-18 01:18 CEST Status: Home page for the unified Equity data-center chain / buildout lens.

docs.title: What this wiki is about
docs.text:
This lens tracks which industrial segments AI / cloud data-center expansion actually propagates through.

Within the unified research system, it serves as the chain entry point for lens-based analysis, not a memo about who is moving the most today: - First, confirm whether chain position is real; - then check whether monetization distance is near or far; - only then ask whether the elasticity-adjusted price signal is worth trading.

docs.title: Why this chain deserves its own wiki
docs.text:
• IEA estimates global data-center electricity use was about 415 TWh in 2024 and could reach close to 945 TWh in the 2030 baseline. The U.S. and China together contribute nearly 80% of the growth. Source: https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/energy-demand-from-ai
  • DOE / LBNL estimates U.S. data-center electricity use was about 176 TWh in 2023 and could rise to 325–580 TWh by 2028, increasing share of total U.S. electricity from about 4.4% to 6.7%–12%. Source: https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-increase-electricity-demand-data-centers

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• These assets determine how borrowing costs and capital-market activity transmit into valuation.
  • Banks, investment firms, and alternative asset managers have very different earnings cycles, so they cannot be mixed.
  • For the cross-sector watchlist, they mostly play the role of discount-rate and risk-appetite transmission.

docs.title: Large integrated banks
docs.text:
• JPM: The thickest balance sheet and highest quality, but valuation remains hard to escape regulatory discounting.
  • BAC: Deposit and wealth-management franchise is strong; watch credit and rate sensitivity closely.
  • HSBC: Asia cross-border network advantage, but geostrategic and restructuring risks are highest.

docs.title: Investment banking and trading
docs.text: • GS: One of the purest names in investment-banking execution; high cyclical beta and high volatility.

docs.title: Alternative asset management / private credit
docs.text:
• BX: Breadth remains the main strength and private-market beta is high, but fundraising and redemption cycles can reverse quickly.
  • APO: Athene provides a permanent-capital amplifier; model is strong, but credit and regulatory complexity is higher.

docs.title: Payment infrastructure
docs.text: • V: Global consumption flow toll collection power; business is strong, but regulation is always close.

docs.title: Core lines I prefer to track now
docs.text:
• In macro uncertainty, JPM and V are better quality observation points.
  • When risk appetite increases, GS, BX, and APO show stronger cyclical beta.
  • HSBC remains a special case with geopolitical and region-specific positioning.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• Regulation and capital requirements can instantly reframe valuation caps for large financial names.
  • Alternative managers look strong in benign credit conditions, but fundraising, redemption, and credit events can compress value and payouts quickly.
  • Payment networks are stable but not immune to regulatory pressure, fee litigation, and large-customer bargaining.

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• These names look “platform-like” at first glance, but in substance this is credit, capital supply, and regulation-driven business.
  • Their volatility often exceeds traditional finance because the market prices growth, tech narratives, and credit quality simultaneously.
  • In the cross-sector lens, they amplify risk appetite and the consumer credit cycle.

docs.title: Digital banking / super apps
docs.text: • SOFI: The most expansive platform-style narrative; user growth, credit quality, and acquisition efficiency determine upside limits.

docs.title: BNPL and flexible payments
docs.text:
• KLAR: One of the strongest mental brands in Europe, but credit, regulation, and competition are heavy.
  • AFRM: Strong merchant distribution and simple core product; funding cost and credit performance remain anchors.

docs.title: AI credit infrastructure
docs.text:
• PGY: More B2B credit infrastructure than consumer-facing; leverage can be meaningful when capital markets stay supportive.
  • UPST: The AI narrative is back, but capital supply and delinquency remain decisive.

docs.title: Retail transaction entry
docs.text: • HOOD: Strong user entry and fast perimeter expansion; transaction volume and regulation can amplify volatility.

docs.title: Main lines I prefer to track now
docs.text:
• For platform expansion in financialization, SOFI and HOOD are more user-entry style names.
  • For credit technology exposure, PGY and UPST are high-beta, high-volatility names.
  • For payments and installment cognition, KLAR and AFRM are closest to direct consumer competition.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• The biggest risk is sudden funding tightening, where many models reveal fragility when liquidity support disappears.
  • Credit quality and regulatory interpretation can quickly change valuation frameworks.
  • Many names are still framed as “platforms,” but the core business remains credit and distribution efficiency.

docs.title: Quick read
docs.text:
• CRDO — Direct; AEC + DSP + optical module route is clear, and it is one of the few interconnect themes the market is truly recognizing. One-line read: [interconnect] AEC/retimer position is concrete; this is a core thread with strong customer concentration.
  • AAOI — Direct / high beta; company has disclosed hyperscaler 800G/1.6T orders and capex plans. One-line read: [interconnect] High-beta optical modules; strong when orders break through, but prone to overheating and pricing pressure.
  • LITE — Direct; Cloud & Networking is now the leading revenue pillar, covering 800G to 1.6T products. One-line read: [interconnect] Legacy optical device name; chain position is strong, but beta is lower than some smaller names.
  • NVTS — Conditional; high-efficiency 10kW platform and AI PSU reference designs fit DC high-voltage upgrades. One-line read: [interconnect] GaN/SiC direction is right, but cash realization is still early. More like an option.
  • MTSI — Conditional / relatively solid; 1.6T/3.2T and AI copper/optical interconnect upgrades provide medium-term demand support. One-line read: [components] Analog and optical devices are more solid; real beneficiaries, but valuation is not cheap.
  • AEIS — Conditional / somewhat direct; Data Center Computing revenue growth is strong, and OCP/ORv3 power architecture aligns with AI load upgrades. One-line read: [power] Strong power-input logic; AI rack power upgrades are real.
  • VICR — Conditional; if high-current low-voltage architecture keeps evolving, its technical moat could be reset upward. One-line read: [high-volatility] Near-rack power architecture advantage; execution is swingy.
  • COHR — Direct; a platform optics company able to participate in 800G, 1.6T, and CPO upgrade layers. One-line read: [interconnect] Core platform optics beneficiary; not just a story. Debt/integration still a burden.
  • GLW — Conditional / infrastructure material; rising data-center cabling and fiber demand gives stable but not the highest beta benefit. One-line read: [materials] Infrastructure material beneficiary with steadier upside and less aggressive beta.

docs.title: Shared discipline
docs.text:
1. First confirm which chain or bucket a company/page belongs to, rather than chasing short-term price moves.
  2. Prioritize primary disclosures, official product pages, annual reports/quarterly filings, and official press releases.
  3. Industry-level theses only calibrate; they do not replace company-level evidence.
  4. Final outputs should be compressed into reusable judgments, not narrative stacks.

docs.title: Source layers
docs.text:
• Frozen TradingView watchlist / normalized manifest: internal watchlist snapshot layer
  • Raw market snapshots: internal market snapshot layer
  • Official IR / annual report / quarterly results / product pages: private primary-document layer
  • Chain-level calibration: IEA, DOE/LBNL, Berkeley Lab, technical media, and others

docs.title: Extra rules for chain-research lens
docs.text:
• Confirm chain position first, then define bull case / risk / one-line judgment.
  • Ask three questions:
  • Who truly resolves the bottlenecks of data-center expansion;
  • Who is just being mapped into the theme;
  • Who has such a long monetization chain that extra risk discount is needed.
  • Classification thresholds:
  • direct: product/service is itself the core bottleneck in data-center expansion.
  • conditional: logic is valid, but monetization strength depends on projects, cadence, or end-user structure.
  • edge: theme-related but mostly mapping, pilot, or non-core revenue.

docs.title: Industry valuation framework
docs.text:
• Platform tech / semis: prioritize forward PE, and use P/S if needed.
  • Financial institutions / capital markets: check earnings quality and regulatory sensitivity first, then PE.
  • Fintech / consumer credit: prioritize P/S, earnings pathway, and source of capital.
  • Pharma / biotech: combine PE, pipeline, patent cliffs, and policy risk.

docs.title: Action mapping
docs.text:
• Buy: top attraction on the current risk/reward setup in this bucket.
  • Hold: still worth monitoring, but current odds, risks, or valuation are not strong enough for top-tier status.
  • Sell: weakest setup in this bucket, or a story too far ahead of execution.

docs.title: Quick read
docs.text:
• BE — Direct; partnerships with Oracle, CoreWeave, and AEP make it one of the most realistic links in the “power shortage” narrative. One-line read: [mainline] Onsite power thesis is real, but the slot is crowded; process discipline matters more than story.
  • FLNC — Conditional / edge; company has publicly framed data centers as one growth driver, and pipeline/backlog offer support. One-line read: [storage] Storage backup has logic but is not a chain core. Watch grid-side execution more closely.
  • STEM — Edge; if campus-level storage and energy management become standard, it has upside. One-line read: [edge] More energy-management mapping than data-center core; quality and continuity are weaker.
  • PSIX — Direct / small-cap equipment supplier; data-center demand is already reflected in financials and management commentary. One-line read: [high-volatility] Fast response power has real linkage; moat is shallow, avoid overestimating persistence.
  • GNRC — Conditional; new hyperscale/colo products and behind-the-meter offerings are now launched. One-line read: [equipment] Backup power / microgrid are real beneficiaries; still industrial equipment, not pure data-center.
  • CAT — Direct / not pure AI; capacity expansion and long-term agreements indicate demand is not pure narrative. One-line read: [equipment] Gas-power and engineering capability can benefit from infrastructure buildout, but not a pure data-center name.
  • BLDP — Edge; Microsoft/Caterpillar-related demos show technical feasibility, so this is not purely conceptual. One-line read: [edge] More hydrogen-fuel-cell story than direct data-center execution.
  • PLUG — Edge; if hydrogen backup commercialization advances, it will have stronger device/system base than pure concept plays. One-line read: [high-volatility] Hydrogen story names; weak direct linkage to data centers.

docs.title: Why this layer is worth separate focus
docs.text:
• Pharma often shows a risk-return profile very different from tech and finance in macro swings.
  • Segmentation matters: health-care services integration, mature pharma, and high-R&D biotech have different valuation frameworks.
  • In this watchlist, this layer behaves more like “cash-flow quality + pipeline + pricing power” in combination.

docs.title: Health-care services integration
docs.text: • CVS: Pharmacy + PBM + insurance integration remains scarce; merger and PBM policy risks cannot be ignored.

docs.title: Large pharma
docs.text:
• LLY: GLP-1 / GIP tailwinds remain strong, with supply, pricing, and overly high expectations as the main offset risks.
  • GSK: Vaccine + specialist-drug mix is improving; if later pipeline steps deliver, repricing room still exists.
  • MRK: Keytruda cash flow remains strong; the key issue is not now but successor throughput after the patent cliff.

docs.title: Biotech platform
docs.text: • REGN: Antibody platform strength is robust and pipeline breadth is wide, but single-product reliance and clinical swing risk are still high.

docs.title: Primary lines I track now
docs.text:
• The clearest high-growth line is LLY.
  • For stable cash flow and valuation transitions, MRK and GSK deserve more attention.
  • REGN is a high-quality platform-style biotech, but with much larger swing risk than large pharma.
  • CVS is closer to policy and utilization-driven trading, not comparable on a simple basis with pure pharma names.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• Drug pricing and reimbursement policy can directly rewrite valuation centers.
  • Pharma and biotech are vulnerable when short-term sales growth is mistaken for durable platform quality.
  • Health-care service integration is more exposed to operations, loss ratio, and simultaneous regulatory deterioration.

docs.title: What this layer covers
docs.text: Platform technology, cloud, internet entry points, and large consumer-tech platforms. The commonality is not that they are “tech stocks,” but that they control traffic entry points, enterprise distribution rights, developer ecosystems, or strong AI-to-platform conversion capability.

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• This group determines whether AI spend turns into real user entry points, enterprise budget allocation, and durable platform lock-in.
  • Their valuation is usually not linear with profits, but with whether platform positioning keeps strengthening.
  • Even with the same “AI beneficiary” label, platform assets have a very different risk structure than pure hardware-chain names: regulators and distribution changes dominate the former, while order cycle and supply cadence dominate the latter.

docs.title: Cloud / Advertising / Consumer platforms
docs.text:
• AMZN: The three-engine system of retail, AWS, and advertising remains strong; execution depends on sustained heavy investment.
  • GOOG: Search cash cow + Cloud AI expansion remain strong; regulatory and capex risk are the main uncertainties.
  • META: Social traffic and ad machine remain the strongest assets; high capex is absorbable, but regulatory shadow remains.

docs.title: Endpoints and enterprise ecosystems
docs.text:
• AAPL: Hardware entry is still powerful, and services plus private AI improve stickiness, but growth remains constrained by device replacement cycles.
  • ADBE: Creative / Acrobat / GenStudio-CX AI workflow layer is real, but after the 2026-05-29 close the action moved from USD232-246 good-buy to pullback-buy / no fresh chase.
  • MSFT: Enterprise software distribution power plus Azure AI is the most complete; expensive, but difficult to replace.

docs.title: Conditional watch position
docs.text: • TSLA: Core business is still automotive and storage, but autonomous driving / robot optionality keeps it within platform-tech watch.

docs.title: Core lines I prefer to track now
docs.text:
• Highest priority remains MSFT, AMZN, and GOOG—names with both distribution power and direct AI budget capture.
  • META looks more like a high-cash-flow platform continuing to apply AI for ad efficiency and retention.
  • TSLA retains interest, but behaves more like a large long-dated optionality position and should not be mixed with the names above.

docs.title: Current main risk
docs.text:
• AI capex is rising across these large platforms; if monetization does not keep pace, valuation compresses first.
  • Antitrust, regulatory, and default-entry changes directly affect the platform premium.
  • Large platforms can be misread as “omniscient”; differences still come from cash flow, distribution power, and ecosystem control.

docs.title: Quick read
docs.text:
• LEU — Conditional; HALEU production and DOE contracts make it a unique position in “Western constrained supply.” One-line read: [power supply] Far-upstream nuclear fuel; long duration and slower monetization. Policy and permitting drive valuation.
  • OKLO — Conditional; headline order book and collaborations with data centers are strong, and the market allows high expectations for long-cycle power. One-line read: [power supply] Long-horizon nuclear power for future power demand; strong story but delayed cash flow. High volatility.
  • TLN — Direct; shortest chain-to-cash path, the most realistic main-line in power. One-line read: [power supply] Ready-to-use nuclear + campus power, most realistic power-chain case. Regulatory and asset concentration are key vulnerabilities.

docs.text: Updated: 2026-06-06 CEST Parent page: Cross-Sector Watchlist Home

docs.title: What this layer covers
docs.text: Semiconductors, chip platforms, storage, and foundational compute-support assets. What matters here is not who has the “AI” label, but who controls non-substitutable links in compute platforms, advanced manufacturing, interconnect, memory, and core analog device layers.

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• Today’s market has less need for “AI storytellers” than for companies that truly deliver compute, manufacturing, interconnect, and memory.
  • Risk profiles vary widely inside this layer: platform firms have higher valuation expectation risk, manufacturing firms face geopolitical and capex risks, and storage firms remain cyclical.
  • This layer typically has the highest upside and the widest dispersion in the watchlist.

docs.title: AI acceleration and platforms
docs.text:
• NVDA: The strongest integrated stack in GPU + software + interconnect, but also the most fully priced.
  • AVGO: Dual positioning in custom XPU and networking gives high beta but high customer concentration.
  • AMD: A complete CPU+GPU platform; execution of Instinct ramp and ecosystem catch-up is the key.

docs.title: Manufacturing / IP / CPU foundation
docs.text:
• TSM: Advanced nodes and advanced packaging are the core substrate, with geographic discount still the largest drag.
  • ARM: It does not sell end-node chips, but provides the software and architecture standard in cloud AI chip development.
  • INTC: A dual bet on products and foundry; odds are high, but execution risk is highest.

docs.title: Connectivity and custom silicon
docs.text: • MRVL: AI infrastructure beta is high, while volatility stems from large-customer rhythm.

docs.title: Storage and memory
docs.text:
• MU: HBM upgrades the story, but memory-cycle characteristics remain.
  • SNDK: Appears more like a storage-cycle + manufacturing JV vehicle than a pure AI-core name.

docs.title: Edge / analog substrate
docs.text:
• QCOM: Physical AI / data-center inference optionality is now stronger than the old AI PC / endpoint-AI frame, but financial proof is not closed; action routes back to the entity and comparison pages.
  • TXN: Important but not high beta, more foundational supply for semiconductors than a pure AI supercycle.

docs.title: Main lines I prefer now
docs.text:
• From a pure platform perspective, NVDA, AVGO, and AMD remain the most worth tracking individually.
  • On foundational scarcity, TSM and ARM determine whether many upstream stories can actually be delivered.
  • On cycle and odds, MU, INTC, and MRVL are more vulnerable to expectation-driven swings.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• Platform names are broadly expectation-heavy; a hyperscaler capex slowdown would pull them back together.
  • For manufacturing and IP foundation, key risks are not demand, but geopolitics, execution, and capex returns.
  • Some storage and parts of edge-compute names can be pulled into AI narratives, but remain constrained by their own cycles and business structures.

docs.title: CVS — CVS Health
docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Pharma and Biotechnology Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Pharmacy network, PBM, healthcare insurance, and care-delivery integration.

docs.title: Why it is in this theme
docs.text: It is not a traditional pharmaceutical company, but it sits directly at the core of U.S. pharma payment, prescription distribution, and insurance administration, making it a healthcare-service integration platform asset.

docs.title: My current preferred bullish case
docs.text: The scale of CVS Caremark PBM, retail pharmacy reach, and insurance-side integration remain scarce; profit recovery resilience should return once Health Care Benefits pressure normalizes.

docs.title: My current key risks
docs.text: Medicare Advantage ratings, healthcare utilization, and PBM policy risk can continue to pressure profits, and the market’s tolerance for complex multi-line integrators remains limited.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: 【Healthcare services】Pharmacy + PBM + insurance integration is still scarce, but MA and PBM policy risk should not be underestimated.

docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-14 23:03 CEST Industry page: Data Center Infrastructure, Power Distribution, and Cooling Classification: Conditional

docs.title: Chain position
docs.text: Dry transformers and power-quality equipment in the low- and medium-voltage distribution segment.

docs.title: Why it is in this chain
docs.text: Not a pure data-center stock, but data-center expansion should lift demand for its custom distribution components.

docs.title: Current bullish logic I am willing to acknowledge

docs.title: Main risk I care about now
docs.text: It is still a slower-cycle equipment supplier; leverage is weaker than purer data-center infrastructure names.

docs.title: One-line conclusion
docs.text: 【Volatility】Transformers and distribution components benefit is real, but this remains a slower-cycle equipment supplier.

docs.title: LEU — Centrus Energy
docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-14 23:03 CEST Industry page: Power Generation and Fuel Supply Classification: Conditional

docs.title: Chain position
docs.text: Advanced nuclear fuel upstream supplier; it sells HALEU/LEU, not direct data-center electricity.

docs.title: Why it is in this chain
docs.text: If advanced nuclear scales in serving data-center loads, HALEU supply becomes a key bottleneck; LEU sits at that upper node.

docs.title: Current bullish logic I am willing to acknowledge
docs.text: HALEU production and the DOE contract place it in a unique position in the “Western constrained supply” narrative.

docs.title: Main risk I care about now
docs.text: The realization path is long; delays in advanced reactor commercialization, licensing, subsidy, or off-take agreements would all pull valuation back.

docs.title: One-line conclusion
docs.text: 【Generation】Nuclear fuel is far upstream; long duration and slow realization. Policy and licensing dominate valuation.

docs.title: LLY — Eli Lilly
docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Pharma and Biotechnology Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Large-cap pharma, metabolism leader, and GLP-1 weight-loss platform.

docs.title: Why it is in this theme
docs.text: Lilly’s most important current asset is not any single drug, but the obesity/diabetes platform unlocked around tirzepatide, along with manufacturing, commercialization, and pipeline expansion it drives.

docs.title: My current preferred bullish case
docs.text: Mounjaro / Zepbound are still scaling rapidly and capacity expansion is catching up; if non-incretin businesses keep growing, Lilly’s earnings structure will be sturdier than many expect.

docs.title: My current key risks
docs.text: The biggest risk is not demand but the combination of supply, pricing, and high expectations; if politics or payer policy start systematic pricing pressure, valuation becomes very sensitive.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: 【Pharma】The GLP-1 / GIP platform is still scaling; the biggest threat is supply, pricing, and over-expectation converging.

docs.title: Key sources
docs.text:

docs.title: META — Meta Platforms
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Platform Technology and Internet Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Social traffic distribution, advertising engine, Meta AI, and AI glasses endpoints.

docs.title: Why it belongs in this theme
docs.text: Its core is not a single social app, but the combination of massive user distribution, ad targeting, and AI consumer entry points.

docs.title: My currently more credible bullish case
docs.text: The Family of Apps still generates very strong cash flow. AI is simultaneously strengthening ad efficiency and user retention; if glasses and assistants scale, the platform perimeter can expand further.

docs.title: My current top risks
docs.text: CapEx is already very high. If Reality Labs and new AI initiatives fail to convert for an extended period, valuation will come under pressure; platform policy and governance risks are also persistent.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: In this Platform model, social distribution and the ad machine remain the strongest assets. High CapEx is manageable, but regulatory overhang is frequent.

docs.title: MRK — Merck
docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Pharma and Biotechnology Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Big-ticket oncology, vaccines, animal health, and a deep late-stage pipeline.

docs.title: Why it is in this theme
docs.text: Merck has a massive cash engine in KEYTRUDA and maintains a deep late-stage pipeline, making it one of the clearest examples of current profit plus long-term replacement in large pharma.

docs.title: My current preferred bullish case
docs.text: KEYTRUDA and WINREVAIR continue to give the company runway; more than 30 phase-3 and over 5 under-review programs show it still has renewal capacity.

docs.title: My current key risks
docs.text: The real issue is not today’s operations but who fills the gap after the patent cliff; if replacement is too slow, the market gives very little leeway.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: 【Pharma】Keytruda cash flow remains strong; the issue is not today, but how fast replacement arrives after the patent cliff.

docs.title: MSFT — Microsoft
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Platform Technology and Internet Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Enterprise software distribution, Azure cloud, and Copilot / agent platform.

docs.title: Why it belongs in this theme
docs.text: Microsoft controls both enterprise workflow distribution and cloud infrastructure, and now AI application delivery; it is one of the clearest enterprise platform technology assets.

docs.title: My currently more credible bullish case
docs.text: Azure and Copilot are pushing Microsoft from software subscriptions toward a higher-ARPU AI platform. Its installed base makes it the most likely candidate to monetize new capabilities quickly.

docs.title: My current top risks
docs.text: CapEx has risen rapidly; if AI monetization is not fast enough, returns will compress. Security incidents, antitrust scrutiny, and pricing pressure from competitors also remain real.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: In this Platform framework, Azure AI and enterprise software distribution are the most complete; expensive, but hard to replace.

docs.title: ORCL — Oracle
docs.text: Updated: 2026-04-14 23:03 CEST Industry page: Cloud and Compute Demand Classification: Direct / Downstream anchor

docs.title: Chain position
docs.text: Downstream demand anchor. Oracle is not a seller of electricity or interconnect equipment, but it is a real AI cloud and data-center campus buyer.

docs.title: Why it is in this chain
docs.text: FY25 Q4 OCI revenue grew strongly year-over-year and RPO kept expanding; multi-cloud expansion and new campus builds imply sustained pull on power, rack, interconnect, and cooling demand.

docs.title: Current bullish logic I am willing to acknowledge
docs.text: Strong order and backlog dynamics; OCI remains in a capex expansion phase and is one of the most realistic demand backdrops for the chain.

docs.title: Main risk I care about now
docs.text: Capex burden is heavy and free-cash-flow could stay pressured; if power availability, delivery, or customer budgets slow, chain spillover will decelerate first.

docs.title: One-line conclusion
docs.text: 【Cloud/Downstream】Database + cloud anchor; AI exposure is real but less high-beta than small-to-mid-cap stocks. Focus on order realization.

It is still not an NVDA/AVGO-style first-line AI infrastructure core.

docs.title: My currently more credible bullish case
docs.text: If AI spills from cloud into endpoints and physical devices, Qualcomm can benefit through low-power inference, connectivity, automotive ADAS/AD, industrial vision, and robotics. If AI200/AI250 and hyperscaler custom silicon convert into named customers, revenue, margin, and backlog, data-center inference/custom silicon adds a re-rating option.

docs.title: My current top risks
docs.text: Phones still anchor margins. FY2026 Q2 handset revenue was down YoY, while data center remains in nonreportable / investment-stage segments. AI200/AI250, HUMAIN, and unnamed hyperscaler work still need customer identity, production revenue, margin, backlog, software ecosystem, and repeatability proof.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: QCOM is now better framed as a Physical AI + data-center inference optionality stock, not only an edge-AI/AI-PC condition stock. Action stays HOLD / no-chase near the old no-chase zone; add only on pullback or after hard revenue/backlog evidence.

docs.title: SNOW — Snowflake
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-05-28 CEST Sector page: Platform Technology and Internet Classification: AI Data Cloud / enterprise data-context / agentic governance platform

docs.title: Thesis position
docs.text: Snowflake sits in enterprise AI's data and context-control layer: Data Cloud, Cortex, Snowflake Intelligence, agentic workflow governance, and consumption-based cloud data infrastructure. It is closer to an AI application data/control plane than to a conventional seat-based SaaS story.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Q1 FY2027 moved the AI story from marketing language toward usage and consumption evidence: product revenue, RPO, million-dollar customers, AI-capability account usage, and the full-year product-revenue guide all strengthened together.

docs.title: Current bull case
docs.text:
Q1 FY2027 product revenue was USD 1.33B, +34% YoY; total revenue was USD 1.39B, +33% YoY; NRR was 126%; RPO was USD 9.21B, +38% YoY; and customers with trailing-12-month product revenue above USD 1M reached 779, +29% YoY. FY2027 product-revenue guidance was raised to USD 5.84B / +31%, and non-GAAP operating-margin guidance was raised to 13.5%.

The more important AI evidence: 13,600+ accounts using Snowflake AI capabilities; Snowflake Intelligence accounts more than doubled QoQ; Cortex Code had 7,100+ accounts. The AWS USD 6B multi-year agreement, OpenAI partnership, SAP capabilities moving to GA, and Natoma / MCP acquisition all support the agentic-enterprise data-context thesis.

docs.title: Key risk
docs.text: The thesis upgrade is real, but the post-earnings price reset is also large. The captured after-hours point near USD 238.88 was about +36% versus the USD 175.26 regular close, implying roughly 15.4x FY2027 guided product revenue on a simple equity-value basis. Snowflake is still a consumption model, so NRR, product revenue, and FCF remain exposed to customer optimization, cloud-budget discipline, and whether AI account adoption converts into durable revenue.

docs.title: Execution bands
docs.text:
Reference: 2026-05-27 regular close USD 175.26; captured after-hours USD 238.88; 200d MA about USD 202.49.

  • USD 185-205: reset buy / preferred pullback around the post-print breakout retest and 200d area.
  • USD 205-225: re-check / small add only.
  • USD 225-250: hold / no fresh chase; the captured after-hours price sits here.
  • USD 260-280: trim / supply unless another guide raise or AI-consumption proof arrives.
  • Failure below USD 200: treat as a failed earnings breakout and re-underwrite product revenue, NRR, RPO, and AI conversion.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: SNOW's Q1 FY2027 was not just a normal beat: it upgraded the AI Data Cloud / agentic enterprise thesis. But the post-print vertical re-rating already prices in a lot of that upgrade, so the action is Hold / pullback-buy / no fresh chase.

docs.title: TSLA — Tesla
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Platform Technology and Internet Classification: conditional

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Consumer technology endpoint, vehicle software, autonomous driving / Robotaxi, energy storage, and robotics optionality.

docs.title: Why it belongs in this theme
docs.text: Its core business remains vehicles and energy storage, but official filings have already positioned FSD, Robotaxi, Optimus, Cortex, and energy software as core technology pathways, so I view it as best monitored under conditional classification.

docs.title: My currently more credible bullish case
docs.text: Energy storage is becoming a second growth leg, and if autonomy and Robotaxi deliver, Tesla can move from a manufacturing story toward a software/platform valuation framework.

docs.title: My current top risks
docs.text: Automotive margins and delivery cadence still determine current cash flow; misalignment between autonomous-driving timelines, regulation, and valuation expectations can be very painful.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: In this conditional lens, the core business is still vehicles and storage, but autonomous driving and robotics optionality justify keeping it in the platform-technology watchlist.

docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-18 01:18 CEST Parent page: Tech Theme Research Alignment with Trade Tracker

docs.title: The scope that should be frozen now
docs.text:
The active scope should satisfy all four conditions: - tech only - scheme first - centered on LLMs and agentic AI - includes the critical chain to actually operationalize this stack: cloud / model production / OS / semiconductors / data-center power & buildout

This means: - The current unified research root still keeps broader sectors like finance and pharma, but Milestone A should not replicate them; - power / buildout providers in the unified research root cannot be excluded because they are part of the current scope, not future scope.

docs.title: The three-layer scheme for Milestone A
1. LLM / agentic AI demand and control layer
docs.text:
Core pages: Platform Technology and Internet, Platform Technology and Internet - Comparison and Scores, Data Center Buildout Home

This layer does not aim to identify every ambush name; it validates: - whether LLM / agentic AI demand continues to expand; - whether AI CapEx continues to convert to real revenue, product usage, enterprise budgets, and platform control; - whether cloud / model production continues to accelerate; - whether OS / distribution control is still concentrated in a few key platforms.

Current names best suited as core anchors: - MSFT — Microsoft - AMZN — Amazon - GOOG — Alphabet - META — Meta Platforms - ORCL — Oracle

docs.title: 2. LLM compute bottlenecks and semiconductor base
docs.text:
Core pages: Semiconductors and Foundational Compute, Semiconductors and Foundational Compute - Comparison and Scores

Focus areas: - GPU / XPU platforms - advanced manufacturing and advanced packaging - HBM / memory - high-speed interconnect and custom silicon - actual LLM training / inference scaling bottlenecks

Current names best suited as core anchors: - NVDA — NVIDIA - TSM — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing - AVGO — Broadcom

More suitable as second-tier / conditional names: - AMD — Advanced Micro Devices - MU — Micron Technology - MRVL — Marvell Technology - ARM — Arm Holdings - MTSI — MACOM

docs.title: 3. LLM / agentic AI data-center buildout chain
docs.text:
Core pages: Data Center Buildout Home

It should be clear: This chain is not only semiconductor spillover; it also includes indispensable power/buildout providers.

Current names most worth including as Milestone A buildout research objects come in two categories:

docs.title: Tech Theme Research Alignment with Trade Tracker - Roles and Feedback Loop
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 20:43 CEST Parent page: Tech Theme Research Alignment with Trade Tracker

docs.title: From a role perspective, which names are anchors and which are more like ambush candidates
Anchor validators
docs.text:
Names that function more as demand / production / bottleneck validators: - MSFT — Microsoft - AMZN — Amazon - GOOG — Alphabet - META — Meta Platforms - ORCL — Oracle - NVDA — NVIDIA - TSM — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing - AVGO — Broadcom - VRT — Vertiv

These names are important for tracker relevance, but mainly provide: - validating whether the main thesis is actually strengthening; - giving valuation and crowding context; - confirming demand for smaller names.

docs.title: Ambush candidates
docs.text: More suitable for prioritizing small/mid/upper-mid names with repricing optionality: - AAOI — Applied Optoelectronics - MTSI — MACOM - CRDO — Credo Technology - FN — Fabrinet - TLN — Talen Energy - BE — Bloom Energy

docs.title: Hard cases / likely false-friend pressure
docs.text: Names to watch carefully because they may look like core names but lack evidence uplift or are already crowded: - COHR — Coherent - OKLO — Oklo - Some optics / power / buildout names where new orders and evidence have not increased in step after becoming too fast

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not use it as a broad US market clue hunter anymore
  • Do not continue introducing finance, pharma, consumer, or other sectors as Milestone A scope
  • Do not treat megacap validation signals as ambush alpha by themselves
  • Do not assume that “semiconductors only” is the scope

docs.title: What to do
docs.text:
First lock tracker to these three schemes: 1. platform-ai-monetization 2. compute-bottlenecks 3. datacenter-buildout-chain

And have it answer only these questions: - Which existing LLM / agentic AI core lines are strengthening? - Which subsegment is upgrading from “story” to “realization”? - Which name is a crowded leader rather than a new ambush setup? - Which small/mid-cap name has “short realization chain + direct evidence + larger repricing room”? - Which power/buildout provider has become an indispensable node in current AI data-center expansion?

docs.title: 1. Wiki is tracker knowledge base
docs.text: Tracker should read from wiki: - scheme ontology - core / conditional / edge classification - current bull case / risk framing - comparison-page method discipline - the relation among cloud / production / OS / semis / power/buildout in the current scope

docs.title: 2. Tracker should write back to wiki
docs.text: When tracker produces reusable findings, it should write back at least: - major scheme-level synthesis - reusable postmortems - why a new ambush candidate should be included - why a crowded leader / false friend should not be upgraded - why a power/buildout name should move from “story” to “real deployment chain”

docs.title: 3. Write-back thresholds still apply
docs.text: Not every alert should become a wiki entry. Only findings that materially change our understanding of the current three schemes are worth recording.

docs.title: Current research boundaries
docs.text: In this stage, explicitly postpone: - Financial Institutions and Capital Markets - Fintech and Consumer Credit - Pharma and Biotechnology - Any cross-industry expansion before the current agentic-AI pipeline is working well

docs.title: Conclusion first
docs.text:
Milestone A should not continue moving toward a broader market discoverer, but it also should not narrow the current scope too much.

The current direction is: - Polish the existing pipeline first; - Lock the current scope to LLMs / agentic AI tech stack + indispensable data-center chain; - Megacaps are more demand / control / bottleneck validators, while small to mid names are the ambush candidate pool.

docs.title: Why the split existed historically
docs.text: On 2026-04-16, the live TradingView watchlist snapshot had 0 overlap with the then-current chain/buildout research root. That justified creating a separate cross-theme watchlist root as a temporary classification gate rather than blindly widening the old chain ontology.

docs.title: Why the merge is now coherent
docs.text: The zero-overlap event is still historically true, but it no longer argues for two active roots. The unified research root now keeps both durable lenses inside one ontology: - Data Center Buildout Home preserves the chain / buildout transmission view - Cross-Sector Watchlist Home preserves the cross-theme watchlist view - both lenses now share one entity layer, one methods page, one query layer, and one active canvas folder
